hypotheses.statement: A channel beyond 1 and 2 identifies an additional distinct human speaker in the recorded audio, most often a third party who takes over or joins the call.
supporting_evidence: Channel 3 and channel 4 both carry conversational turns that interleave with channel 1 and channel 2 in source order and are answered by the channel 1 speaker.
Several units contain an explicit hand-over: the channel 1 speaker asks whether the person talking is the line owner or 'the lady before', which only makes sense with at least three participants.
Channels 3 and 4 each carry their own non-speech event records (UNCLASSIFIED / SONANT / LAUGH), i.e. the vendor tracked them like any other speaker, not like a system stream.
Record timestamps never overlap channel 1 or channel 2 records, the same non-overlapping rule that holds between channels 1 and 2.
counter_evidence: The corpus carries no speaker attribute, so 'distinct speaker' is a structural inference from turn-taking, not a verified label.
Channel 5 carries only two event records and no speech at all, so it cannot be a speaker under this hypothesis in the observed data.
benchmark_implications: Third-party turns may contain business-relevant information (who is the owner, what the owner wants).
Treating the third party as 'customer' would silently merge two different people into one speaker role.
Treating the third party as 'historical_agent' is worse: it would put customer-side words into the agent's mouth.

hypotheses.statement: The channel number is a per-unit speaker slot assigned by the transcription vendor, so channel 1 is not *guaranteed* to be the agent and channel 2 is not *guaranteed* to be the customer in every unit; the 1=agent, 2=customer mapping is a corpus-level regularity.
supporting_evidence: At least three valid units have no channel 1 speech at all while the channel 3 speaker delivers the agent's opening script and product pitch, and the channel 2 speaker answers as the customer.
In those units the channel 1 records are SYSTEM / DTMF / ENS events plus pre-call room audio, which is exactly the role channel 1 plays elsewhere when the agent speaks on channel 1.
Across units the same channel can act as agent-side or customer-side, which a fixed physical-leg interpretation does not predict.
counter_evidence: The effect is rare: only 3 of 4,527 units lack channel 1 speech, and 99.8% of units start on channel 1.
No external call record exists to confirm which speaker is the agent, so this rests on content reading, not on ground truth.
benchmark_implications: The current task builder rejects any cutoff whose visible prefix contains an 'other' channel, which is the conservative response and needs no change before human review.
A future approved change that maps an unknown channel to a role must be applied per context, not as a global constant, and must be validated unit by unit.

hypotheses.statement: An unknown channel carries IVR prompts, ring-back or recorded system announcements rather than a live speaker.
supporting_evidence: The corpus already models non-speech audio as explicit events (SYSTEM / MUSIC / DTMF) and those events are attached to channels 1 and 2, so a channel is not intrinsically a speech-only stream.
Channel 5 carries only two UNCLASSIFIED events and no speech.
counter_evidence: Channels 3 and 4 carry ordinary conversational Chinese that is answered by the channel 1 speaker, which a recorded announcement would not produce.
The corpus has no channel value whose records are exclusively system events except channel 5, and even there the sample is 2 records.
benchmark_implications: Even if true for channel 5, the effect on the benchmark is zero: event records are already excluded from visible context.

hypotheses.statement: Unknown-channel records are a recording or transcription artifact (echo, duplicate capture, overlapping-speech split) rather than new content.
supporting_evidence: Some channel 4 records duplicate the immediately preceding channel 1 or channel 2 wording, which is consistent with an ASR boundary artifact.
counter_evidence: The corpus contains zero overlapping records, so an unknown channel never coincides in time with channel 1 or 2.
Most channel 3 and channel 4 speech contains content that does not appear on any other channel.
Unknown-channel records carry their own event records and their own truncation markers, which a pure duplication artifact would not.
benchmark_implications: If duplication were confirmed, deduplicating would change turn counts but not the visible prefix semantics.

hypotheses.statement: An unknown channel is a second agent-side leg, such as a supervisor monitoring or a colleague consulted during the call.
supporting_evidence: One unit opens with two alternating speakers complaining about calling customers before the called party answers, which reads as two colleagues in the same room.
One unit has a channel 3 speaker delivering the agent script while channel 1 holds only events.
counter_evidence: In most units the unknown-channel speaker answers the agent's questions in the customer's role, not the agent's.
No supervisor or consultation event marker exists in the corpus.
benchmark_implications: A second agent leg would break the assumption that exactly one historical agent turn follows a customer turn.

limitations: The corpus carries no speaker attribute (role=UNKNOWN everywhere), so no channel meaning can be confirmed from the data alone.
The de-identified corpus drops the source gender/language attribute, so per-channel voice profile cannot be measured here.
Channel 5 has two records, both events: two records cannot support a statistical characterisation.
Timestamps are offsets from the start of the recording, not wall-clock times, so absolute placement in the call flow is unavailable.
No external call record or vendor channel specification is available in the workspace to confirm any hypothesis.
